clue.text: Bob, once getting manual protection, is infatuated

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; 'is infatuated' means 'is smitten'

parts.note: a bob was the old British shilling, abbreviated s before decimal coinage
a glove that protects the hand

explanation.surface: Someone from the old days, now gloved up, has fallen in love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name, but a bob was slang for a shilling, the pre-1971 British coin written s.
explanation.definitionFit: Being smitten is being struck with love, a common informal synonym for helpless romantic attraction.

clue.text: Name of Russian organisation: Let's Goad American Leaders?

indicators.note: the leaders of a group of words are their opening letters, the ones at the front

parts.note: the first letter of each of these four words

explanation.surface: A Russian agency's name is mocked as a slogan urging people to provoke Americans.
explanation.definitionFit: Olga is a traditional Russian woman's given name, borne by saints and princesses.

clue.text: see 27dn.
(&25dn.) Put up with old-style Labour faction and start a U-turn?

parts.note: to bear something is to tolerate it
the Labour left wing, the party's socialist faction before New Labour

explanation.surface: A jibe that tolerating Labour's old left means the party reversing course.
explanation.walkthrough: The political U-turn of the surface becomes a literal driving one: you begin turning round by steering to one side.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear left is to steer gently leftward, a plausible opening move when swinging a car round in a road.

clue.text: Yoof-like escalation — grabbing benefit

indicators.note: something grabbing another thing holds it inside its grasp

parts.note: the dole is British slang for unemployment benefit

explanation.surface: Youth culture is blamed for a rise in claims on welfare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yoof' is a mocking British spelling of youth; the definition is an adjective describing the young.
explanation.definitionFit: Adolescent describes teenagers, the age group mockingly called 'yoof' in British slang.

clue.text: Mission statement opening spikes M&S and ebay's wrangling

indicators.note: to spike something is to stick a point into it, so one piece goes inside another
wrangling is quarrelling and tangling, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the retailer's initials and the auction site's name, joined by 'and'

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A corporate mission statement disrupts a squabble between high-street and online retailers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mission statement' reads as one phrase but splits: Mission is the definition. M&S is Marks & Spencer, the British department store.
explanation.definitionFit: A diplomatic mission is the body of envoys and their building abroad, the same thing as an embassy.

clue.text: Forces Archer to protect one drunk?

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it

parts.note: Mary Archer, scientist and wife of the novelist and Tory peer Jeffrey Archer

explanation.surface: Jeffrey Archer is ordered to look after someone who has had too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Archer' suggests Jeffrey, but it is his wife Mary, a favourite Private Eye target, who wraps round the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The military means the armed forces collectively: army, navy and air force together.

clue.text: Get pissed, all round right pissed: it'll make you tread warily

indicators.note: going all round something means enclosing it on every side

parts.note: to tope is to drink heavily

indicators.note: pissed here means drunk, and a drunk word staggers into a jumbled order

explanation.surface: A drinker is warned that getting very drunk makes walking a careful business.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'pissed' is part of a definition of TOPE; the second is the anagram signal working on right.
explanation.definitionFit: A tightrope walker must place every step with great care, so the wire forces cautious footing.

clue.text: Endlessly market the unfinished Millennium flop? Not that often, actually

indicators.note: without its end, the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to market goods is to sell them

indicators.note: something not finished lacks its last part, so the final letter goes

parts.note: the Millennium Dome in London, a famously unpopular 2000 exhibition

explanation.surface: An attempt to sell off the failed Millennium Dome rarely comes to anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Seldom means rarely or infrequently, an adverb matching the phrase about something happening not very often.

clue.text: Savour cupping woman's top then tweak suspender elastic?

definitions.note: a verb phrase; the answer is the verb

indicators.note: cupping something means holding it inside curved hands

parts.note: a savour is a sharp taste

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A saucy seaside-postcard scene: a fondle followed by a snap of stocking elastic.
explanation.definitionFit: To twang is to pluck something taut so it vibrates with a ringing sound, as a stretched strap would.

clue.text: Country person underneath Clinton in a state

parts.words: Country person underneath Clinton in a state
parts.note: surface reading: a rural figure lying beneath Bill Clinton, in a flustered state, a nod to his intern scandal
setter's reading: a nation whose people live Down Under, a federation made up of states

explanation.walkthrough: 'Underneath' points to the nickname Down Under, and 'in a state' to the nation's division into states rather than to anyone's agitation.
explanation.definitionFit: The country nicknamed Down Under is organised as a federation of six states and two territories.

clue.text: As love article (sexy top) gives relief

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A racy magazine feature with a revealing top offers comfort.
explanation.definitionFit: To soothe is to calm or ease pain, the same as bringing someone relief from discomfort.

clue.text: Shifting Carter involved taking one

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside
something involved is intricate and tangled, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A former US president caught up in some scheme brings someone along.
explanation.definitionFit: Erratic behaviour moves unpredictably and changes course, so it is constantly shifting.

clue.text: A ruthless Thatcher associate's balls were lit outrageously?

parts.note: balls is slang for nonsense, as is rot

indicators.note: acting outrageously means behaving wildly out of order

explanation.surface: A hardline Thatcher minister's nonsense was wildly lit up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is British slang for rubbish talk, not anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard-nosed enforcers in Thatcher's cabinet were nicknamed after the aggressive guard-dog breed.

clue.text: Un-PC woman's body mangles his sac balls finally

definitions.note: the label marks it as an old-fashioned slang sense

indicators.note: mangling something twists it out of shape
finally points to the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A crude description of a woman's figure doing painful damage to a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Chassis is dated, sexist slang for a woman's figure, borrowed from a car's frame.

clue.text: An absorbing process as perverse Kate secures independence

indicators.note: perverse means turned the wrong way, so the preceding word runs backwards
securing something means holding it fast inside

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for independence or independent

explanation.surface: A supermodel's twisted behaviour keeps her free of others.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology the term names the gradual seepage of a solvent through a membrane, a process of soaking up.

clue.text: Pissed with Nick's place (created to cause maximum disturbance)

definitions.note: describes the idiom 'create merry hell', a phrase rather than a noun

parts.note: merry is a mild word for tipsy
Old Nick is the Devil, whose home is the underworld

explanation.surface: A drunk turns up at the Devil's home intent on chaos.
explanation.definitionFit: To create or play merry hell is an idiom for raising an uproar or causing great trouble.

clue.text: John Major's right wing sore at devious means of "Islamification"?

indicators.note: devious means winding and indirect, so the letters wander out of order
the right wing of a word is its right-hand end, its final letter

explanation.surface: Tory right-wingers are aggrieved at an alleged scheme to impose Islam.
explanation.walkthrough: John Major was a Conservative prime minister; 'right wing' looks political but takes only the end of his surname. The 2014 'Trojan Horse' affair alleged Islamist takeovers of Birmingham schools.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trojan horse is a hidden means of subversion from within, the name given to that alleged school plot.

clue.text: Clap: the result of getting laid — put out

indicators.note: out here means put out of place, disordered

explanation.surface: A crude joke: catching the clap is what sleeping around leads to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clap' looks like slang for a venereal disease, the result of getting laid, but it means applause.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaudit is an expression of praise, originally a round of applause, so a clap.

clue.text: Oldie Stone at last comprehending internet etc. rock

indicators.note: comprehending in its old sense means taking in or including
at last points to the final letter of the word before

parts.note: information technology, of which the internet is an example

explanation.surface: An elderly Rolling Stone finally grasps the internet and rock music.
explanation.definitionFit: Granite is a hard igneous stone, a classic example of the material geologists call rock.

clue.text: Perfect? Not Rolf ultimately — criminal, actually

indicators.note: not means without, so that letter is taken away
ultimately points to the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Rolf Harris, the entertainer later jailed for sex offences, was far from perfect.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawless conduct disregards legal rules, so it is criminal in character.

clue.text: Unreliable counsel from Chuck: rest uneasily

indicators.note: something lying uneasily shifts about restlessly

explanation.surface: Bad advice from a man named Chuck leads to sleepless nights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck' poses as a name but is a verb meaning throw.
explanation.definitionFit: A shyster is a dishonest lawyer, so a counsel whose integrity cannot be trusted.

clue.text: Film producer luvvies ran amok (very lacking)

indicators.note: running amok is rampaging wildly out of control
lacking means missing, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: v is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: Luvvies, theatrical types, went wild on a film set with little restraint.
explanation.definitionFit: Universal Pictures is a major Hollywood studio that makes and distributes movies.

clue.text: Evasive characters, arses: hard to be got rid of

indicators.note: getting rid of something removes it altogether

parts.note: heels are contemptible people, as are arses
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Slippery types, the idiots, are difficult to shake off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' suggests people; it is literal creatures that wriggle away.
explanation.definitionFit: Eels are proverbially slippery fish that wriggle free of a grasp, hence elusive creatures.

clue.text: see 4dn.
The ambushed politician's face might have … to be far from deterring

definitions.text: The ambushed politician's face might have …
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a politician pelted with eggs literally has yolk on the face

definitions.note: a participle phrase defining a verb, fair because 'far from deterring' reads as the act of urging on
definitions.meaning: second meaning: urging someone forward, the opposite of discouraging

explanation.surface: A politician hit by protesters is unlikely to be put off.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg someone on is to urge them to act, and having egg on your face means being embarrassed.

clue.text: (& 3dn.) Rather doubtful thing, head, in the case of oldies?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an issue that is neither clearly right nor wrong

definitions.text: head, in the case of oldies
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the part of an old person that has gone silver

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is whimsical: an elderly person's hair has turned colourless, so the head is literally an ashen zone.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase denotes an ambiguous matter not clearly covered by rules, hence something doubtful.

clue.text: The very best you can hope for ladies is being messed about

definitions.text: The very best you can hope for
definitions.note: a singular-looking phrase defining a plural, fair because 'the very best' can stand for several hoped-for things at once

indicators.note: something messed about is disordered and jumbled

explanation.surface: A cynical remark that the best women can expect is poor treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideals are standards of perfection, the highest outcomes one could wish or aim for.

clue.text: Rejected sports body: glib, awash with money

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back the way it came

parts.note: the Football Association, English football's governing body

explanation.surface: A smooth-talking, cash-rich football authority is turned down.
explanation.definitionFit: Affluent people are wealthy, with plenty of money flowing in.
